title: Comparative reading: who should choose the expert witness?
bodyMd:
**Passage A**

An expert witness is chosen by a party, paid by that party, and prepared for testimony by that party's lawyers. We should not be surprised that experts so selected tend to say what the party that selected them wants said. The distortion need not involve dishonesty. A lawyer consults several candidates and retains the one whose preliminary view is most favourable; the retained expert then reports that view sincerely. Selection alone, operating on an entirely honest population, produces a systematically skewed sample of opinion in the courtroom.

The remedy is therefore structural rather than moral. Where a field has a body of specialists whose judgments can be compared, the court should appoint its own expert from a roster maintained by a professional body, with the parties free to examine that expert and to call their own in addition. Jurors would then hear at least one opinion whose content was not a condition of the speaker's employment. Objections that this makes the court's appointee unduly influential mistake the proposal: an appointed expert who is wrong can be cross-examined like any other.

**Passage B**

Reformers who worry about who hires the expert have fixed on the wrong variable. Consider toolmark comparison, in which an examiner concludes that a mark left at a scene was made by one particular implement. For decades examiners testified to such matches in categorical terms, and for decades no study established how often an examiner reaches that conclusion wrongly. The trouble was never that the examiners were paid by the prosecution. It was that the technique had no measured error rate, so that no honest examiner could have said how much weight the conclusion deserved.

Appointing such an examiner from a neutral roster would not have supplied the missing number. It would have removed the one check the adversarial system does provide — an opposing expert with an incentive to say that the emperor has no clothes — and replaced it with the court's own imprimatur. Neutrality is no substitute for validity; where a method is unvalidated, neutrality is an aggravating factor, because it lends the method the authority of the court. The reform worth pursuing is a threshold requirement that a technique's error rate be measured before any opinion resting on it is admitted at all.
accessibilityText: Two short prose passages presented as a pair, labelled Passage A and Passage B, each of two paragraphs. Passage A argues that because expert witnesses are selected and paid by the parties, selection alone skews courtroom opinion even among honest experts, and proposes that courts appoint their own experts from a professional roster in fields where specialists' judgments can be compared. Passage B argues that the identity of the person who hires the expert is the wrong variable, using toolmark comparison as its example: the real defect was the absence of a measured error rate, and a court-appointed examiner would remove the adversarial check while adding the court's authority to an unvalidated method. Passage B proposes instead that a technique's error rate be measured before opinions based on it are admitted. There are no figures, tables or mathematical notation.

provenance.notes: Both passages written from scratch for this item bank as a comparative-reading pair. Not adapted from, and not a paraphrase of, any LSAC comparative set or any published article or court opinion. Toolmark comparison is used as a generic category of forensic pattern evidence; no specific study, report, case or author is cited or reconstructed.
